title: Bulgur: What It Is, How to Cook It, and How It Differs From Couscous

seo.title: Bulgur: What It Is, How to Cook It, and Bulgur vs. Couscous
seo.meta_description: Bulgur is whole wheat that has been precooked, dried, and cracked. It cooks quickly because it is already parboiled. Unlike couscous, it is cracked grain rather than tiny semolina pasta.
seo.search_intent: Understand what bulgur is, how to cook different sizes, why it cooks so quickly, and how it differs from couscous and raw cracked wheat.

excerpt: Bulgur is not a separate grain species. It is wheat that has been cleaned, precooked, dried, and cracked into different sizes. That processing explains its short cooking time. Unlike couscous, bulgur remains cracked wheat grain rather than granulated pasta.
content_html:
Bulgur is wheat that has been cleaned, precooked, dried, and then cracked into different sizes. It is not a separate cereal species. When the bran, germ, and endosperm remain in their original proportions, bulgur qualifies as a whole-grain form of wheat.

The precooking step is what makes it unusually fast. The Whole Grains Council explains that bulgur has already been boiled and dried before sale, so it needs much less cooking than an intact wheat berry.

Bulgur is different from raw cracked wheat

Cracked wheat can simply mean raw wheat kernels broken into smaller pieces. Bulgur, by contrast, has been cooked before drying and cracking.

The difference may be hard to see in a bag, but it changes cooking dramatically. Raw cracked wheat still needs longer hydration, while bulgur can become tender in minutes.

Bulgur is not couscous either

Traditional couscous is made by moistening durum-wheat semolina and forming it into tiny pasta granules. Bulgur remains the wheat kernel itself, only precooked and broken.

Both can appear in salads, side dishes, and herb-heavy recipes, which explains the confusion. Their textures differ: bulgur has a more obvious grain-like chew and a nuttier whole-wheat flavor.

How do you cook medium or coarse bulgur?

The Whole Grains Council uses 1 cup bulgur to 2 cups water or broth as a reference, simmered for roughly 10–12 minutes and yielding around 3 cups cooked.

A simple method is to bring liquid to a boil, add bulgur, lower the heat, cover, and cook until tender. Resting briefly afterward and fluffing with a fork helps separate the grains.

Fine bulgur may only need soaking

Small particles are already precooked and water has only a short distance to travel. Some fine bulgur can be prepared simply by pouring hot water over it and letting it stand.

This is especially useful in tabbouleh, where the goal is tender but distinct grains. Boiling very fine bulgur for too long can turn it soft and pasty.

Grind size changes the best use

Fine bulgur works well in salads, fillings, and herb mixtures. Medium and coarse bulgur are better for pilafs, side dishes, soups, and meals where you want a more noticeable chew.

Size labels are not completely standardized across manufacturers, so package directions are more reliable than assuming every product needs exactly the same amount of water and time.

Do you need to rinse bulgur?

Many modern products are cleaned and ready to cook, so rinsing is not always necessary. If the package recommends it or you see loose powder, a quick rinse can remove surface dust.

Drain thoroughly because retained rinse water contributes to total hydration and can make a small batch softer than expected.

Why is bulgur common in tabbouleh and pilaf?

Its fast cooking, firm texture, and whole-wheat flavor let it absorb dressings without immediately falling apart. In tabbouleh it supports parsley, tomato, lemon, and olive oil; in pilaf it absorbs broth and spices.

It can also substitute for rice or couscous when you want a more rustic grain texture.

Bulgur is wheat, so it contains gluten

Being whole grain or minimally processed does not make it gluten-free. Bulgur is wheat and contains gluten proteins.

The practical rule: treat bulgur as precooked cracked wheat. For medium bulgur, start around 1 part bulgur to 2 parts liquid and about 10–12 minutes; for fine bulgur, check whether hot-water soaking is enough.

For repeatable results, use the same variety or brand and change only one variable at a time. Grain size, moisture, flour quantity, and cooking method can all change the final texture substantially, so your own reference is more useful than chasing one universal number.

faq.question: What is bulgur?
faq.answer: Bulgur is wheat that has been precooked, dried, and cracked into different sizes.

faq.question: Are bulgur and couscous the same?
faq.answer: No. Bulgur is cracked wheat grain, while couscous is usually tiny pasta made from durum semolina.

faq.question: How much water does bulgur need?
faq.answer: For medium bulgur, about 2 parts liquid to 1 part bulgur is a useful starting reference, although size and brand can change it.
